blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Most system design interviews ask you to build a product that happens to sit behind a load balancer, a URL shortener, a chat app, a video platform, and the load balancer is treated as a box you draw once and never open again. This document flips that. The system being designed here is the load balancer itself: the thing every other system in this kind of interview quietly assumes already exists and just works.

Think about what a load balancer actually does, stripped of the jargon for a second. Picture a small doctor's office with one receptionist and ten waiting patients, but three doctors sitting idle in three different rooms. The receptionist's entire job is to glance at who just walked in, notice which doctor is free or about to be, and send the patient to the right room, all in the time it takes to say a name out loud. A load balancer is that receptionist, except instead of ten patients an hour it might be handling a hundred thousand requests a second, and instead of three doctors it might be routing across a fleet of servers spread across multiple continents, and it has to make that same fast decision correctly, every single time, without ever becoming the reason the whole office grinds to a halt.

1.1 What exactly are we building

At its core, this is a distributed system that accepts inbound connections on behalf of a pool of backend servers, spreads each one across that pool using a configurable algorithm, continuously verifies which backends are actually healthy, optionally terminates TLS on the client's behalf, and, critically, does all of this without itself becoming the single point of failure that everything else in the architecture now depends on.

That last clause is the twist that makes this problem genuinely interesting rather than a checkbox exercise. Every other system in this course gets to treat its load balancer as a solved problem sitting outside the design. Here, the load balancer is the design, and it has to solve its own high availability problem using the exact same tools, redundancy, health checking, and failover, that it hands out to everything behind it.

blocks.text: 2.1 The must-haves
blocks.content: 2.1 The must-haves

["Accept and distribute traffic: take incoming connections or requests on behalf of a pool of backend servers and hand each one to exactly one healthy backend.","Support both L4 and L7 modes: raw TCP/UDP forwarding for protocols that need it, and HTTP-aware routing on path, header, or cookie when the workload calls for it.","Run a choice of algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, consistent hashing, and IP hash, selectable per backend pool.","Continuously health check every backend: detect a failing instance and pull it from rotation automatically, then restore it automatically once it recovers.","Add, remove, and reweight backends with zero downtime: a fleet that is constantly scaling up and down cannot require a restart of the load balancer to reflect that."]
items: Accept and distribute traffic: take incoming connections or requests on behalf of a pool of backend servers and hand each one to exactly one healthy backend.
Support both L4 and L7 modes: raw TCP/UDP forwarding for protocols that need it, and HTTP-aware routing on path, header, or cookie when the workload calls for it.
Run a choice of algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, consistent hashing, and IP hash, selectable per backend pool.
Continuously health check every backend: detect a failing instance and pull it from rotation automatically, then restore it automatically once it recovers.
Add, remove, and reweight backends with zero downtime: a fleet that is constantly scaling up and down cannot require a restart of the load balancer to reflect that.

blocks.text: 2.2 The features that make it production-grade
blocks.content: 2.2 The features that make it production-grade

["TLS termination and passthrough: decrypt once at the edge when backends should not have to manage certificates, or forward encrypted traffic untouched when they must.","Session persistence: optionally pin a client to the same backend across a session, for the backends that are not yet fully stateless.","Graceful connection draining: let in-flight requests on a backend finish before that backend is removed, instead of cutting them off mid-response.","Observability: per-backend and per-node metrics, request logs, and health status, all exposed in a form a monitoring system can consume.","An administrative API: a programmatic way to register backends, change weights, and adjust routing rules without touching a config file by hand."]
items: TLS termination and passthrough: decrypt once at the edge when backends should not have to manage certificates, or forward encrypted traffic untouched when they must.
Session persistence: optionally pin a client to the same backend across a session, for the backends that are not yet fully stateless.
Graceful connection draining: let in-flight requests on a backend finish before that backend is removed, instead of cutting them off mid-response.
Observability: per-backend and per-node metrics, request logs, and health status, all exposed in a form a monitoring system can consume.
An administrative API: a programmatic way to register backends, change weights, and adjust routing rules without touching a config file by hand.

blocks.text: 3.1 Scalability
blocks.content: 3.1 Scalability

blocks.text: The load balancer tier has to scale horizontally with traffic, adding nodes as request volume grows, without any single node becoming a ceiling on the whole system's throughput.

blocks.text: 3.2 Availability
blocks.content: 3.2 Availability

blocks.text: This is the requirement that matters more here than in almost any other system design problem. If the load balancer is down, everything behind it is unreachable, no matter how healthy those backends actually are. The load balancer has to be more available than the services it protects, not merely as available.

blocks.text: The load balancer itself should add negligible latency to every request it touches, ideally well under a millisecond for the routing decision, since that overhead is paid on every single request that flows through the system, forever.

Routing state can afford to be eventually consistent across nodes; a client's actual request cannot afford to be dropped.

blocks.text: 5.1 Traffic assumptions
blocks.content: 5.1 Traffic assumptions

blocks.text: This design assumes a large web platform with 20 million daily active users, averaging 100 requests per user per day, spread across a mix of HTTP and HTTPS traffic. It assumes backends are mostly stateless but that a meaningful minority still rely on session persistence, which is exactly the tension explored in depth in §16. Traffic is assumed to be bursty rather than flat, with peaks running roughly five times the daily average.

blocks.text: 5.2 Business and system constraints
blocks.content: 5.2 Business and system constraints

It is assumed that backends expose a lightweight health endpoint the load balancer can probe, and that a control plane, however small, exists to hold configuration and backend registry state durably.

blocks.text: 6.2 How much state does a single LB node hold in memory
blocks.content: 6.2 How much state does a single LB node hold in memory

blocks.text: Assume roughly 5% of daily active users are connected concurrently at any given peak moment, thanks to HTTP keep-alive holding connections open between requests. That is 20,000,000 * 0.05, or 1,000,000 concurrent connections spread across the entire fleet at peak. Each connection entry, a five-tuple, the backend it is pinned to, a little bit of session bookkeeping, weighs in at around 250 bytes. Spread evenly across a fleet of roughly 30 active nodes, that is about 33,333 connections per node, times 250 bytes, or a little over 8 megabytes per node. Trivial, and it is worth sitting with why: unlike a database holding petabytes of business data, a load balancer's own state is deliberately small, which is exactly what makes it possible to fail one node over to another in seconds rather than minutes.

blocks.text: 6.3 Bandwidth
blocks.content: 6.3 Bandwidth

blocks.text: Assume an average request plus response pair weighs around 2 kilobytes combined. At the peak of 115,000 requests a second, that is 115,000 * 2 kilobytes per second, or roughly 230 megabytes a second, about 1.86 gigabits, in aggregate across the whole fleet. Spread across 30 nodes, that is under 8 megabytes a second per node, comfortably inside even a modest network interface. The real constraint on a load balancer node is almost never raw bandwidth, it is CPU spent on TLS handshakes and the number of new connections it can accept per second, which is exactly why §16.12 spends real time on the termination-versus-passthrough decision.

blocks.text: 7.3 Reading that diagram left to right
blocks.content: 7.3 Reading that diagram left to right

blocks.text: Follow the arrows in the overall diagram and the whole design falls into place. A client request enters through anycast DNS, which resolves to whichever regional load balancer pair is actually closest to that client. The active node in that pair does the real routing work, while the passive standby sits idle, exchanging heartbeats, ready to take over the moment the active node stops responding, the exact mechanism covered in full in §16.13. Off to the side, the health checker is constantly probing every backend and writing status changes into the config store, which is the same store the admin API writes to when an operator registers a new backend or changes a weight. Every data-plane node polls or subscribes to that config store, so a health status flip or a weight change shows up on the next request, not on the next deployment. Metrics flow out asynchronously onto a queue toward monitoring, which is why that edge is drawn separately from the request-serving path itself.

blocks.content: 7.4 Control-Plane Microservices Architecture

blocks.alt: Zooming into the control plane: an admin API, a backend registry service, a health check service, and a config distribution service each own one narrow job

blocks.text: Zooming into "the control plane" as a single blob hides an important decision: it is not one application, it is a handful of small, independently deployable services, each owning one narrow responsibility. The backend registry service owns the authoritative list of backends and their metadata, backed by its own database. The health check service only ever writes probe results into that registry, it never talks to a client. The config distribution service takes a versioned snapshot of the registry and pushes it out to every data-plane node, so a node restarting mid-deploy always picks up a known-good version rather than a half-written one. Splitting these apart means a slow health check service, say because a backend is timing out on probes rather than responding, can never block a completely unrelated weight update from an operator going through the admin API.

blocks.text: 11.1 SQL vs NoSQL for the control plane
blocks.content: 11.1 SQL vs NoSQL for the control plane

blocks.text: Look closely at how the registry from §10 actually gets used: config distribution reads it in full, in bulk, on every push cycle, and the admin API writes to it one backend at a time. There are no complex joins in the hot path, and the total number of rows, even at a fleet of thousands of backends, is small enough that a relational database handles it without breaking a sweat. A plain relational table, with the composite index from §10.1, is a perfectly reasonable choice here, arguably the simplest one that still gives strong consistency for what is genuinely a small amount of authoritative state.

At that scale, a key-value or wide-column store partitioned by pool_id plays more naturally with horizontal scaling than a single relational instance does.

blocks.content: 16.1 L4 vs L7: what is the actual difference
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208126597-359196555.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208126597-359196555.png
blocks.alt: An L4 balancer sees only the IP address and port of a packet, while an L7 balancer reads the entire HTTP request

blocks.text: An L4, transport-layer, load balancer makes its routing decision purely from the IP address and port in a packet header. It has no idea what HTTP path is being requested, what cookie is attached, or what the request body contains, and it does not need to, it is just forwarding connections. That ignorance is a feature: with nothing to parse, an L4 balancer can push enormous throughput at very low latency, and it works equally well for protocols that have nothing to do with HTTP at all, raw TCP services, UDP-based game servers, database connections.

That intelligence has a cost: parsing HTTP, and usually terminating TLS to be able to read it at all, is meaningfully more CPU-expensive per request than L4's simple byte forwarding.

blocks.text: 16.2 Round robin
blocks.content: 16.2 Round robin

blocks.text: The simplest algorithm there is: cycle through the backend list in order, one request each. Three identical backends, A, B, and C, receiving nine requests, get exactly three apiece. It works beautifully precisely when its one assumption holds: every backend has equal capacity and every request costs roughly the same to serve. The moment either of those stops being true, round robin quietly starts sending equal shares of traffic to unequal machines, which is exactly the gap weighted round robin closes.

blocks.text: 16.3 Weighted round robin
blocks.content: 16.3 Weighted round robin

blocks.text: Give each backend a weight reflecting its actual capacity, say a 5 vCPU instance gets weight 5, a 3 vCPU instance gets weight 3, and a smaller 2 vCPU instance gets weight 2, and the algorithm should send traffic in that same 5 to 3 to 2 proportion rather than splitting it evenly. Naive weighted round robin does this by just repeating each backend weight times in a row, A, A, A, A, A, B, B, B, C, C, which technically hits the right ratio but bursts five requests at the biggest backend before touching anything else, exactly the kind of momentary imbalance a smoothed version avoids.

Naive weighted round robin does this by just repeating each backend weight times in a row, A, A, A, A, A, B, B, B, C, C, which technically hits the right ratio but bursts five requests at the biggest backend before touching anything else, exactly the kind of momentary imbalance a smoothed version avoids.

blocks.text: The smooth version used by servers like nginx tracks a running current weight per backend, adds each backend's static weight to it on every pick, selects whichever backend now has the highest running total, and then discounts that winner by the total weight across all backends. Tracing it by hand for weights 5, 3, and 2 across ten picks produces the sequence A, B, C, A, A, B, A, C, B, A, five A picks, three B picks, two C picks, matching the configured ratio exactly, while never sending more than two of the same backend back to back. That smoothing is the entire reason production load balancers use this version instead of the naive one.

blocks.text: 16.4 Least connections
blocks.content: 16.4 Least connections

blocks.text: Round robin and weighted round robin both assume every request costs roughly the same to serve, and that assumption breaks the moment request duration varies a lot. Picture backend A already holding 40 long-lived connections, maybe it is serving a handful of slow, streaming responses, while backends B and C are sitting at 5 connections each. Round robin would still cheerfully send every third new request to A, piling onto an instance that is already the most loaded one in the pool. Least connections instead looks at the live connection count on each backend and always picks whichever one currently has the fewest, correctly steering new traffic toward B and C until the numbers even back out.

blocks.text: 16.5 Least response time
blocks.content: 16.5 Least response time

blocks.text: Least connections is a good proxy for load, but it is still only a proxy. Picture backend D holding just 2 connections, each one a slow, 800 millisecond database-heavy query, next to backend E holding 10 connections, each a fast 20 millisecond lookup. Least connections alone would favor D, the exact opposite of what should happen, since D is actually the more overloaded machine per unit of useful work. Least response time factors in actual measured latency alongside connection count, and correctly favors E despite its higher raw connection number, because E is demonstrably the more responsive backend right now.

blocks.content: 16.6 Consistent hashing for cache-affinity workloads

blocks.alt: A key lands on the hash ring and gets assigned to whichever backend node sits next going clockwise

blocks.text: None of the algorithms above care which specific backend a given request lands on, only that load stays even. Some workloads care a great deal. A caching tier is the classic example: if requests for a given user's session data can land on any backend at random, every single backend ends up holding a partial, mostly-cold copy of that user's data, and the underlying database gets hit far more than it should.

A caching tier is the classic example: if requests for a given user's session data can land on any backend at random, every single backend ends up holding a partial, mostly-cold copy of that user's data, and the underlying database gets hit far more than it should.

blocks.text: Consistent hashing solves this by placing every backend at several points, virtual nodes, on a hash ring spanning a fixed numeric range, say 0 to 2 to the 32nd. A request key, say user:8842, hashes to a point on that same ring, and gets routed to whichever backend owns the next point clockwise from it. Every request for that same key lands on that same backend, every time, for as long as the ring does not change, which is exactly the affinity a cache-heavy workload needs.

blocks.text: The real payoff shows up when the backend set changes. Add a fourth cache node to a ring that previously had three, and only the keys that happen to fall between the new node's position and its immediate predecessor move, roughly one over the new total number of nodes of all keys, not the whole keyspace. Compare that to a plain modulo hash, hash(key) % N, where changing N from 3 to 4 reshuffles almost every key at once, since the modulus itself changed. That difference, a small, bounded reshuffle instead of a near-total one, is the entire reason consistent hashing exists.

blocks.text: 16.9 Health checking: active probes vs passive detection
blocks.content: 16.9 Health checking: active probes vs passive detection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208132926-889921503.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208132926-889921503.png
blocks.alt: A backend moves from healthy to suspect to unhealthy and only back to healthy after a run of consecutive successful probes

blocks.text: Active health checking means the load balancer independently reaches out to every backend on a fixed interval, hitting a lightweight endpoint like /healthz, and judges health purely from that probe's outcome. It catches a backend that has quietly wedged itself even if no real traffic happens to be flowing to it at that exact moment. Passive health checking instead watches real requests as they flow through, if a backend starts timing out or returning errors on actual traffic, it gets marked down without ever needing a dedicated probe. The strongest designs run both together: active checks catch a silently broken backend before a real user ever reaches it, and passive checks catch the failure modes an artificial probe endpoint might not reproduce, like a specific slow database query path that only real traffic exercises.

blocks.text: 16.10 How fast can you safely mark a backend unhealthy
blocks.content: 16.10 How fast can you safely mark a backend unhealthy

blocks.text: There is real tension buried in this question. Mark a backend down after a single failed probe, and one dropped packet on an otherwise healthy instance yanks it out of rotation for no good reason, a phenomenon called flapping. Wait too long, requiring ten consecutive failures before acting, and real users keep getting routed to a genuinely broken backend the entire time.

Mark a backend down after a single failed probe, and one dropped packet on an otherwise healthy instance yanks it out of rotation for no good reason, a phenomenon called flapping. Wait too long, requiring ten consecutive failures before acting, and real users keep getting routed to a genuinely broken backend the entire time.

blocks.text: A practical middle ground, and the one assumed throughout this document, checks every backend every 2 seconds, and requires 3 consecutive failures before marking a backend unhealthy, which pulls a truly broken backend out within about 6 seconds. Recovery is made deliberately slower than failure: 2 consecutive successes are required before a backend is trusted again, roughly 4 seconds of sustained good behavior, which is asymmetric on purpose, quick to distrust, a little slower to trust again, and that asymmetry is what keeps a marginal, barely-recovering backend from bouncing in and out of rotation every few seconds.

blocks.text: Here is the problem worth being honest about: sticky sessions actively fight against horizontal scalability. A backend that is quietly overloaded cannot shed its pinned clients to a less busy neighbor, they are stuck there by design. Worse, if that one backend dies, every session pinned to it dies too, there is no other instance holding a copy of that state to fail over to. The real fix is not a cleverer stickiness algorithm, it is removing the need for stickiness entirely by moving session state into a shared store like Redis that any backend can read, which is the direction every mature system eventually moves in, sticky sessions are usually a stepping stone, not a destination.

blocks.content: 16.12 SSL/TLS termination vs passthrough

blocks.alt: Terminating TLS at the load balancer decrypts once and forwards plain traffic inward, while passthrough keeps every hop encrypted

blocks.text: Termination means the load balancer holds the certificate, completes the TLS handshake itself, and forwards plain, unencrypted traffic inward to the backend. This centralizes certificate management in one place and gives the L7 routing engine something it can actually read, which is a prerequisite for path-based routing at all. Passthrough means the load balancer never decrypts anything, it just forwards the encrypted bytes, and the backend itself terminates TLS. This keeps traffic encrypted for the entire hop, which some compliance regimes require, but it also means the load balancer is flying blind, an L4 passthrough setup cannot route on an HTTP path it has never actually read.

blocks.content: 16.13 The load balancer's own single point of failure problem

blocks.alt: An active load balancer holds the virtual IP while a passive standby waits, ready to claim it the moment a heartbeat stops arriving

blocks.text: This is the twist called out back in §1: everything so far has assumed the load balancer itself is always there. It is not, by default, it is one more machine that can crash, run out of file descriptors, or lose network connectivity, and unlike a single backend failing, a load balancer failing takes down every single backend behind it at once, healthy or not.

It is not, by default, it is one more machine that can crash, run out of file descriptors, or lose network connectivity, and unlike a single backend failing, a load balancer failing takes down every single backend behind it at once, healthy or not.

blocks.text: The classic fix is active-passive failover around a shared virtual IP address. The active node holds that IP and serves all traffic. The passive node sits idle, exchanging a heartbeat with the active node every second or two. The instant that heartbeat stops arriving, typically within a few seconds, the passive node claims the virtual IP for itself and starts serving traffic, and clients, who only ever knew about the IP address, not which specific machine held it, never have to be told anything changed.

The instant that heartbeat stops arriving, typically within a few seconds, the passive node claims the virtual IP for itself and starts serving traffic, and clients, who only ever knew about the IP address, not which specific machine held it, never have to be told anything changed.

blocks.text: 16.14 Multi-LB fronting: DNS-based vs anycast-based
blocks.content: 16.14 Multi-LB fronting: DNS-based vs anycast-based
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208149576-729245744.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785208149576-729245744.png
blocks.alt: DNS-based routing hands the client several addresses to choose from, while anycast lets the network itself route the same address to the nearest healthy location

blocks.text: Active-passive failover solves for one load balancer dying. It does nothing for an entire region going dark. Two broader strategies handle that. DNS-based multi-LB returns multiple A records, one per region, and lets either the client or a DNS-level health check decide which one to actually use, simple to reason about, but bound by DNS TTLs, a resolver can keep handing out a dead region's address for as long as its cache says that answer is still valid. Anycast takes a different approach entirely: the exact same IP address is announced from every region at once, and the network's own routing layer, via BGP, sends a client's packets to whichever announcing location is topologically closest and currently healthy. Anycast reacts to a regional failure in the time it takes routes to reconverge, typically seconds, rather than waiting out a DNS TTL that could be minutes.

blocks.text: The load balancer sits at the network edge, which makes it both the first line of defense for everything behind it and the first thing an attacker actually touches. Its own admin API needs real authentication and authorization, mutual TLS or signed API keys backed by role-based access control, since anyone able to call it can silently redirect an entire pool's traffic. blocks.text: 21.1 How the load balancer defends against a flood
blocks.content: 21.1 How the load balancer defends against a flood

blocks.text: A SYN flood tries to exhaust a server's connection table by opening huge numbers of half-finished TCP handshakes and never completing them. SYN cookies defend against exactly this: instead of allocating real state for every incoming SYN, the load balancer encodes enough information into the SYN-ACK response itself to reconstruct the connection only once the client actually completes the handshake, which means a flood of never-completed connections costs almost nothing to absorb. Layered on top of that, per-client connection rate limiting catches abusive but technically valid traffic, and for genuinely large volumetric attacks, beyond what the LB fleet alone can absorb, the honest answer is routing through an upstream scrubbing service or a provider-level DDoS protection layer sitting in front of the anycast tier itself.

blocks.content: 24.3 Software vs hardware vs cloud-managed

blocks.text: A hardware appliance, the kind vendors sold for decades before cloud load balancing matured, offers predictable, dedicated performance but is expensive, slow to scale, since scaling means buying another box, and turns into its own fleet-management problem at real scale. blocks.text: 27.1 Testing this before it ever reaches production
blocks.content: 27.1 Testing this before it ever reaches production

blocks.text: A routing config change is exactly the kind of thing that should never go straight from zero traffic to everything at once. The weight-update API from §9.4 makes a canary rollout a first-class operation: push a new backend or a new algorithm configuration at a small weight, watch its error rate and latency against the existing fleet for a fixed observation window, and only ramp it up toward full weight once it has proven itself. If it has not, rolling back is just another weight update, not an emergency deploy. The same mechanism doubles as the safe way to test an entirely new load-balancing algorithm in production, on a small, real slice of traffic, before trusting it with all of it.

items: "How would you support WebSocket connections that need to stay open for hours?" Treat them as an L4 concern once the initial HTTP upgrade handshake completes, and make sure health checks and connection draining both account for a connection that is expected to be long-lived rather than assumed dead after a normal timeout.

"What happens if the health check endpoint itself is slow, but the rest of the backend is fine?" That is exactly why passive detection in §16.9 matters alongside active probing, a probe endpoint is still just a proxy for real health, not a guarantee of it.

"How would you roll out a completely new load-balancing algorithm with zero downtime?" The canary mechanism from §27.1, at a small weight, watched, ramped gradually, exactly as it would for a new backend.

"What if two regions each think they are the primary during a network partition?" That is the split-brain scenario named in §26.1, resolved through quorum-based arbitration rather than letting either side keep serving unilaterally.

"How would you rate-limit individual clients without penalizing everyone behind a shared corporate NAT?" Move the rate-limiting key from raw IP to something more specific, an API key or a session token, whenever the client can supply one, and fall back to IP only when it cannot.
